Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision–Language–Action Models

Abstract

Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with π0\pi_{0}, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.

1 Introduction

Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly place a reasoning stage between perception and action (Zawalski et al., 2024; Hao et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a), and this intermediate state empirically improves policy success rate. This intermediate state is attractive because it can separate what the robot decides to do from the motor trajectory that realizes that decision. Yet existing reasoning models represent this state as one vector per observation. This raises the question: should a model expose one committed decision per observation, or a distribution over valid ones?

The distinction matters whenever the observation leaves more than one decision valid. Consider a robot facing two identical cubes, with an instruction that names neither: nothing favors one target over the other. The same ambiguity is pervasive in everyday tasks: whether to pick up a can or push it aside, how to grasp a mug, or which route to take. A reasoning state that must produce a single decision necessarily collapses these alternatives. Averaging them may yield an invalid plan between the cubes; choosing one avoids this failure but still hides the equally valid alternative. The missing property is therefore not simply validity, but a representation that preserves the alternatives so they remain accessible at inference time, allowing preferences or outcomes to dynamically select the most viable strategy at deployment without retraining (Figure 1). We call a reasoning state addressable when, at inference time, the policy can be: sampled to obtain distinct valid decisions (coverage), conditioned to select among them a single decision (steering), and reweighted by outcome to adapt the decision in closed-loop (outcome adaptation). The limitation of prior designs is therefore a lack of addressability. This is not the usual action-multimodality problem: robot learning has already developed generative action models precisely to avoid averaging incompatible motor trajectories (Section 2). The unresolved question is whether the upstream decision should itself also be represented as a distribution.

We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (gpl), which replaces a deterministic plan readout with a conditional distribution pθ​(z∣c)p_{\theta}(z\mid c) of plans zz given a VLA representation cc. This distribution can be sampled, steered toward a requested mode, and reweighted from deployment experience, all without retraining the underlying VLA. We show that the plan provides a substantially stronger handle than the action distribution for expressing an external preference. Under matched executors, selecting a requested plan increases the fraction of executions that follow it from 0.48 to 0.94, whereas applying the same inference-time intervention to π0\pi_{0}’s native action distribution yields no reliable improvement. Because these alternatives remain explicit, deployment outcomes can also change which plans are preferred without updating the plan generator or VLA. This benefit is conditional: an explicit plan can influence behavior only when it carries decision information that the executor cannot already recover from the observation. We call this the redundancy principle. In a controlled test, changing only the demonstrations to reduce this redundancy increases the plan-selection effect from +0.19 to +0.65. Finally, these capabilities do not depend on hand-designed plan coordinates: they persist when the plan representation is learned directly from demonstrated behavior.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We identify the decision bottleneck as a distinct locus for multimodality in VLAs and define addressability, the capacity to preserve alternative decisions so they can be sampled, selected, and revised. Matched plan- and action-level interventions show that the decision bottleneck provides the stronger handle for controlling behavior.

  • •

    We introduce gpl, a distribution over task-level plans, instantiated by a rectified-flow head and integrated into π0\pi_{0} with frozen base weights and a small adaptation.

  • •

    We propose the redundancy principle: an explicit plan should affect behavior only when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.

2 Related Work

Reasoning in VLAs.

Recent VLAs increasingly insert an intermediate reasoning stage between perception and action. Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) (Zawalski et al., 2024) makes this reasoning explicit in language, grounded in robot-relevant quantities such as subtasks, objects, and motion; other approaches move this computation into continuous hidden states (Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a; Bai et al., 2026; Tur et al., 2026). CoT-VLA (Zhao et al., 2025) instead samples visual subgoals as sequences of future frames, yielding a visual chain-of-thought in pixel space rather than a compact plan representation. Despite these different representations, continuous action-domain reasoners typically expose a single intermediate state per observation (Table 2), rather than an explicit distribution over alternative decisions.

Continuous and generative latent reasoning.

Continuous reasoning was first studied in the language domain: Coconut (Hao et al., 2024) feeds hidden states back into the model as continuous thoughts, while generative approaches place a distribution over the reasoning state (Ye et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2026; Tu et al., 2026). STAR-LDM (Lovelace et al., 2025) similarly samples a latent reasoning state that is injected as soft tokens before generation. These works establish continuous and stochastic reasoning for text.

Latent plans and generative planning.

Sampling latent plans to condition low-level control is well established in robot learning (Lynch et al., 2019; Lynch & Sermanet, 2021; Mees et al., 2022). Higher-level policies can search these spaces (Rosete-Beas et al., 2022), while LDCQ (Venkatraman et al., 2024) learns a multimodal distribution over latent skills and selects among them with a value function. Trajectory-level generative planners (Janner et al., 2022; Ajay et al., 2023) combine sampling with test-time guidance, while SuSIE (Black et al., 2024b) and UniPi (Du et al., 2023) generate visual subgoals for downstream control.

Generative actions and adaptation.

Generative action models (Florence et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024; Chi et al., 2025) and flow-based VLAs (Black et al., 2024a) already represent multimodal motor behavior. Flow-reversal and noise-space methods (Wagenmaker et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026) steer these action distributions, while verifier-based selection (Kwok et al., 2025), rejection-based post-training (Tan et al., 2025), reinforcement-learning-style updates (Chen et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025), and failure- or energy-guided action generation (Zheng et al., 2026; Song et al., 2026) use feedback to improve behavior.

Together, these lines of work provide intermediate reasoning states, generative latent plans, and multimodal action distributions, but leave open where multimodality should reside in a reasoning-augmented VLA.

3 Method: The Generative Plan Latent

The change relative to a standard VLA.

A modern VLA may already be generative at the action level; our method does not replace that machinery. Instead, we insert a generative variable upstream of the action model, at the point where the task-level decision is represented. Figure 2 traces the resulting pipeline: the frozen VLA backbone reads the observation and instruction into a conditioning vector, the generative plan latent samples and projects the task-level decision from that conditioning, and the action expert consumes the projected plan alongside fresh observations to act at every step.

Problem setting.

Let oo denote an image observation and ll a language instruction. A pretrained VLA backbone fϕf_{\phi} maps them to a conditioning representation c=fϕ​(o,l)c=f_{\phi}(o,l). We define a plan z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} as a low-dimensional representation of the decision required by the task as opposed to the motor trajectory that accomplishes it.

Generative plan model.

We model the conditional plan distribution p⁡(z∣c)p(z\mid c) with rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023b; Lipman et al., 2023). With z0∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), t∼𝒰⁡[0,1]t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1] and zt=(1−t)​z0+t​zz_{t}=(1-t)z_{0}+tz for a plan zz extracted from a demonstration, a velocity field vθv_{\theta} is trained with

ℒplan​(θ)=𝔼c,z,z0,t​‖vθ​(zt,t,c)−(z−z0)‖22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{plan}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{c,z,z_{0},t}\left\|v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)-(z-z_{0})\right\|_{2}^{2}. (1)

At inference we draw z0z_{0} from the prior and integrate with the Euler method to obtain z∼pθ​(z∣c)z\sim p_{\theta}(z\mid c); because this takes only a handful of integration steps rather than a token-by-token decode, one latent-plan draw costs roughly 80×80\times less than one sampled reasoning chain in a matched comparison on the same conditioning and backbone (ECoT-VLA, Zawalski et al. (2024)). A projector PηP_{\eta} maps the sampled plan to k=8k=8 soft tokens [e1,…,ek][e_{1},\ldots,e_{k}] inserted into the executor prefix, the plan interface, after which the executor predicts its action chunk using its native action objective.

Steering.

Suppose a user specifies a desired plan property yy, such as which object to grasp or which route to follow. We train a lightweight noise-conditioned classifier qψ​(y∣zt,t,c)q_{\psi}(y\mid z_{t},t,c) on intermediate noisy plans along the flow path and bias the velocity field with its score during inference:

vguide​(zt,t,c,y)=vθ​(zt,t,c)+w​∇zt​log⁡qψ​(y∣zt,t,c),v_{\mathrm{guide}}(z_{t},t,c;y)=v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)+w\,\nabla_{z_{t}}\log q_{\psi}(y\mid z_{t},t,c), (2)

where w≥0w\geq 0 controls guidance strength. Setting w=0w=0 recovers the original plan distribution while increasing ww moves probability mass toward the requested mode, and neither the plan generator nor the VLA is retrained when the command changes (Section 4.2).

Outcome adaptation from experience.

Steering assumes that the desired plan property is specified externally; outcome adaptation instead uses feedback obtained after deployment, while keeping the plan generator fixed. Let z(1),…,z(K)∼pθ​(z∣c)z^{(1)},\ldots,z^{(K)}\sim p_{\theta}(z\mid c) be candidate plans and let s⁡(c,z)s(c,z) denote a deployment-time score, with larger values preferred. Outcome adaptation reweights the plan prior toward high-scoring candidates:

padapt​(z∣c)∝pθ​(z∣c)​exp⁡(β​s​(c,z)),p_{\mathrm{adapt}}(z\mid c)\propto p_{\theta}(z\mid c)\exp\!\left(\beta s(c,z)\right), (3)

where β≥0\beta\geq 0 controls how strongly deployment feedback modifies the plan prior. The score ss is deliberately generic, and we evaluate two broad classes of scoring mechanisms (formalized in Section F.1). A learned critic trains a parametric model s⁡(c,z)=gω​(z)s(c,z)=g_{\omega}(z) to predict rewards directly from accumulated (z,r)(z,r) deployment rollouts, where rr is the deployment outcome associated with zz. Alternatively, when a task partitions into discrete modes, a non-parametric reward table simply assigns a candidate plan the historical average reward of its corresponding mode, requiring zero training floating-point operations (FLOPs). Rather than greedily executing a single top-scoring draw, both methods reweight the discrete candidate pool with Boltzmann weights; reported performance is the resulting expected outcome. Both scoring mechanisms can continuously absorb new deployment experience to update their estimates, while the generative prior pθ​(z∣c)p_{\theta}(z\mid c) and the underlying VLA remain completely fixed.

Adapting a pretrained VLA.

While the GPL is designed to augment any modern pretrained VLA, we instantiate our primary architecture using π0\pi_{0}. To integrate the generative plan without disrupting the underlying capabilities of the backbone, we add a projector and a low-rank adapter (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2021) to the action expert. This adapter is trained purely through the native action objective of the VLA without requiring an auxiliary plan-imitation loss. To ensure the executor remains robust, we use classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho & Salimans, 2022), so we randomly drop plan tokens during training. We evaluate against three strict baselines: the unmodified stock π0\pi_{0}, a plan-less control (which uses our adapted weights but omits the plan at inference), and a dedicated no-plan adapter trained at an identical budget. Full details are in Section B.2.

4 Three Capabilities of an Addressable Plan

Setup.

We deploy our method across two distinct executor pipelines. To isolate reasoning from execution confounds and enable extensive ablation matrices, we first use a learned soft-token executor featuring a frozen perception backbone and a flow action head trained from scratch. For external validity, we then evaluate on a pretrained VLA (π0\pi_{0} or π0.5\pi_{0.5}), adapted as described in Section 3.

4.1 Coverage: Representing the Full Decision Space

Coverage asks whether the reasoning state preserves all valid decisions rather than merely returning one valid point. We therefore compare GPL not only with a deterministic mean-squared-error (MSE) readout, which can average incompatible modes, but also with a winner-take-all (WTA) selector that commits to the most likely valid mode without maintaining a distribution. We test this on a square-footprint object that admits two valid top-down orientations 90∘90^{\circ} apart. As detailed in Table 1, the deterministic MSE baseline averages the two modes into a diagonal grasp that misses the object entirely. While WTA nearly eliminates invalid predictions, it collapses to a single mode and fails to cover all available decisions. GPL, instead, successfully captures both valid modes across all layouts. This shows that avoiding an invalid mean is insufficient and that true coverage requires preserving the alternative decisions.

4.2 Steerability: The Plan Is the Stronger Handle

While coverage exposes alternatives, steerability asks whether a user can choose among them without retraining the base models, and whether the locus of that guidance matters. We report the commanded-mode rate, the fraction of episodes whose executed decision matches the request, and the steer range, i.e., difference between opposite commands.

The plan distribution can be steered.

On the two-object task, where training demonstrations are perfectly balanced between the two modes, the requested mode is executed with probability 0.410.41 without guidance. By using a lightweight noise-conditioned classifier to bias the plan flow toward a requested mode at inference time, we achieve a steer range of +0.57+0.57 at the canonical operating point.

The plan is the stronger intervention point.

A VLA offers two natural alternatives for steering behavior: specifying the desired decision through the language instruction, or intervening directly on the generative action expert.

We first compare GPL against guidance of π0\pi_{0}’s native action distribution. Since a generative action expert already represents multiple possible motions, a central question is whether an additional distribution over plans provides a meaningfully better control interface. For this action-level baseline, we use the dedicated no-plan adapter, trained on the same task and at the same adaptation budget as the GPL executor. As shown in Figure 3, GPL’s commanded-mode rate rises monotonically from 0.48 to 0.94, whereas action-chunk guidance produces no within-arm gain whose interval excludes zero and declines above w=2w=2. The relevant decision is explicit in plan space, but is distributed across many action dimensions and timesteps once expressed as a motor trajectory.

We next evaluate gpl against an ECoT-style language baseline. Both methods issue commands to the identical downstream executor and are evaluated on the same closed-loop success metric: successfully grasping and lifting the specified target cube. Across three adapter seeds and 4040 held-out spatial configurations, gpl achieves a steering range of +0.54+0.54, whereas the language baseline manages only +0.02+0.02. We find that downstream execution competence is not the bottleneck: the language baseline actually grasps objects more reliably than the plan-based approach (0.500.50 versus 0.330.33 overall success rate), yet it systematically fails to follow the specific target command. Furthermore, when opposing steering signals are applied simultaneously, the continuous plan dictates the executed target cube in all 240240 evaluation rollouts. Equipping the language baseline with a matched trainable projector causes its overall grasp rate to collapse entirely, so its steering range cannot be interpreted (Section E.3).

4.3 Outcome Adaptation: Can Experience Change Which Plans Are Selected?

While steering specifies a preference externally, outcome adaptation uses deployment experience to infer which plans should be preferred. If unseen deployment dynamics invalidate a previously viable strategy, for example, a larger object causing grasps to fail while pushing remains effective, a policy that preserves multiple plans does not need to relearn how to act. gpl enables this by reweighting the plan distribution using the agent’s own rollout outcomes, shifting toward plans that remain effective.

Experience can optimize among already-valid plans.

In a three-object rearrangement task, where an object should be placed in its dedicated position identified by the color, the plan dictates the execution order. Because every permutation validly completes the task, the frozen generator learns them all equally and stays blind to any preference cost. At deployment, we introduce an additional preference that was absent from training: minimizing the chained end-effector path length required to execute the full ordering. We fit a lightweight critic on rollouts from the model itself to score each order. We deploy this as our first task-specific instance of the shared mechanism: a continuous cost regressor to minimize physical penalties. Because the learned gωg_{\omega} is continuous, it can score unseen plans at the cost of fitting ω\omega. As shown in Figure 4A, Boltzmann-reranking candidate plans at inference time drastically reduces the expected regret, whereas a shuffled-cost control shows no improvement. Naturally, the deterministic baseline, being a single plan, cannot be reranked.

Why rerank plans rather than action samples?

Since π0\pi_{0} is a generative policy, a natural alternative is to sample and rerank raw action trajectories directly. A no-plan π0\pi_{0} baseline, matched in scenes, capacity, and critic architecture, fails to reduce execution costs, and the gap favoring plan-level reranking widens as the sample budget (KK) increases. The reason is executable diversity: action-diffusion noise mostly produces small variations of one committed strategy rather than independently successful alternatives (Section F.2).

Reranking can avoid further generator training.

Returning to the two-cube task, we introduce a hidden reliability objective: the two geometrically valid targets have asymmetric, unobserved success probabilities, and the agent sees only a binary outcome after each grasp. We rerank frozen plan samples with no generator gradient steps, via either a learned critic (a small regressor fit on the observed outcomes) or a reward table (a smoothed per-mode average, fit-free). As illustrated in Figure 4B, both generator-frozen arms match continued behavior cloning (Continued-BC) and Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) (Peng et al., 2019), both of which update the flow generator on the same deployment rollouts, within a strict statistical equivalence margin. The critic reaches parity at ≈388×{\approx}388\times fewer training FLOPs, and the reward table needs none at all. Construction of the hidden-cost objectives, cross-scene validation, the reranking-locus ablation, and the FLOP accounting are given in Appendix F.

5 When Does the Plan Matter? The Redundancy Principle

In robotic manipulation, an explicit plan can improve task success only to the extent that it carries decision-relevant information the executor cannot already read from the observation. If the observation alone dictates the decision, the plan is redundant. In such cases, its benefits vanish while its interface overhead remains, potentially degrading net success. Conversely, when ambiguity, occlusion, or distributional shifts leave the decision open, the plan becomes load-bearing and must be addressable. We quantify this redundancy with R~=1−H⁡(y∣c)ln⁡m\widetilde{R}=1-\frac{H(y\mid c)}{\ln m}, where H⁡(y∣c)H(y\mid c) is the held-out cross-entropy of a probe predicting the decision yy from the conditioning cc of the executor, and mm is the number of modes, assumed marginally uniform (Section G.2). Thus R~≈0\widetilde{R}\approx 0 indicates little information about the decision, while R~≈1\widetilde{R}\approx 1 indicates it is nearly determined by cc. Three monotone manipulations test whether the effect of the plan tracks this score.

Ambiguity.

Sweeping the training distribution under a fixed scene and executor reveals that the generative advantage (success-rate gap over the deterministic baseline) scales directly with task ambiguity (Figure 5). Performance shifts from a net penalty in unambiguous tasks to substantial gains under full bimodality. A strictly unimodal control confirms the source of this penalty: when initial observations fully resolve the decision, an intermediate plan provides no new information, acting purely as an architectural bottleneck.

Occlusion and commitment.

Next, we test temporal redundancy by hiding the target visual mesh from time tt onward during a π0\pi_{0} manipulation task. As occlusion destroys decision information in the observation, committing to a previously selected plan becomes critical. Carrying an early plan through the occlusion heavily outperforms both stock π0\pi_{0} and the matched plan-less control (by up to 36 and 28 percentage points, respectively). It also decisively beats re-inferring the plan from the degraded image at every step (Figure 5). Importantly, this gain tracks the privileged-state ceiling: when occlusion happens late (or not at all), the observation remains sufficient, the plan becomes redundant again, and the baselines converge.

A causal test on LIBERO.

LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a) provides our sharpest causal test. To strictly isolate whether the plan carries the decision, we use generic language instructions that omit specific target names. This requires deploying pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Black et al., 2025) rather than π0\pi_{0}. Because π0\pi_{0} overfits to verbatim fine-tuning strings, it completely collapses under generic instructions (dropping to just 3/3003/300 successes), leaving no headroom to measure the effect of the plan. In contrast, π0.5\pi_{0.5} robustly follows generic commands (retaining 140/300140/300 successes) owing to its broader pretraining, providing the necessary competent baseline (Appendix G). However, when the plan generator is trained purely on π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s default habit rollouts, the resulting plan is largely redundant with the scene (R~=0.47\widetilde{R}=0.47, measured prior to adapter training) and steering is accordingly weak. We intervene by replacing only these habit demonstrations with counterfactual pairs (e.g., placing either bowl in the identical visual context) to deliberately break the observation-decision correlation, holding the executor, benchmark, and adaptation recipe strictly fixed.

Modifying these training demonstrations solely to drive the redundancy score from 0.47 down to 0.00 improves the pooled oracle steer range from a weak effect (+0.19) to a strong effect (+0.65) across all six matched adapter seeds. Furthermore, across a five-point dose sweep constructed from intermediate mixture levels, redundancy and steering performance exhibit a perfect inverse rank correlation (Spearman’s ρ=−1.00\rho=-1.00; Table 13).

Consequently, the unguided learned sampler recovers its steering capability, and counter-habit outcome adaptation becomes positive across all counterfactual seeds (compared to just one of six habit seeds). An ablation that altered instruction wording without changing R~\widetilde{R} left the effect unchanged. Ultimately, redundancy predicts whether the executor will use the plan, not whether the architecture is globally cost-free: non-redundancy makes the plan valuable, while the conditioning interface itself can impose an independent competence cost (reported in Section 7).

6 Generality Across Plan Representations and Domains

The addressability results in Section 4 have so far been demonstrated only with hand-designed plan coordinates and in a single simulator, SimplerEnv Li et al. (2024). We test both dependencies here.

6.1 Does Addressability Require Hand-Designed Coordinates?

Addressability is not an artifact of hand-designed plan coordinates. While our previous experiments relied on structured plans with explicitly defined modes, here we replace those labels with a 2-D plan latent learned entirely from behavior. We train an autoencoder to compress demonstrated future end-effector trajectories into this space, using only outer-train layouts and freezing it before any object, mode, or language labels are introduced. We then train the same generative flow and deterministic heads over the frozen learned latents.

All three addressability operations remain viable without hand-designed coordinates (Figure 6). Offline, the generative flow covers both valid targets on most held-out scenes, whereas the deterministic readout falls off-mode on nearly 75% of its predictions. Thus, despite being learned entirely from data, the resulting latent space remains both steerable and rerankable. In closed-loop execution through π0\pi_{0}, guiding the learned plan latent raises the commanded-mode rate from the stock-π0\pi_{0} baseline of 0.50 to 0.78, approaching the 0.92 oracle-code ceiling obtained when the executor is given the encoded ground-truth path. This oracle ablation effectively decouples the downstream fidelity of the executor in following the latent representation from the upstream accuracy of the generative flow in producing it. Most importantly, under identical adapters and scenes, the learned plan latent is statistically indistinguishable from the hand-designed 3-D anchor in closed-loop steering (paired difference +0.03+0.03), despite somewhat lower offline coverage. Thus, addressability does not require predefined or human-readable plan coordinates: in this setting, a compact representation learned directly from demonstrated behavior is sufficient.

6.2 Schemas, Embodiments, and Domains

The three capabilities are not tied to one simulator, one embodiment, or one domain. A single 54-D schema of object-relative contact events (position, approach angle, gripper state), trained jointly across four SimplerEnv task families, recovers valid alternatives on all four (Section H.1). On RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024), a mobile-manipulator embodiment with a different simulator, scene distribution, and robot, an offline probe with fixed plan anchors shows that π0\pi_{0} realizes both commanded alternatives, and reranking raises plan-level task success from 0.65 to 1.00, though terminal mobile-base navigation remains outside the scope of the adapted executor (Section H.2). Beyond manipulation, the framework extends to an abstract multi-path maze domain using a higher-dimensional route-map plan (Appendix C). In this setting, the learned plan space supports coverage, steering, and outcome adaptation over multiple feasible routes through the maze.

7 Limitations and Scope

Three limitations define the current scope of the addressability results. First, all experiments are conducted in simulation. The main effects are observed across three simulators and an abstract maze domain, but we have not yet tested them on hardware. Second, existing manipulation benchmarks rarely provide the kind of underdetermined decisions needed to study multimodality directly. We therefore construct most of the multimodal settings used here, including the two-cube and three-object tasks, the contact-sketch scenes, and the LIBERO counterfactual demonstrations. Pretrained VLAs do not always adapt well to this shift. On LIBERO, π0\pi_{0} achieves only 3/3003/300 successes under the generic instructions required by the test, which motivates our switch to π0.5\pi_{0.5}. Even with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, none of the four preregistered magnitude predictions are met. Removing the redundancy hypothesized to drive this degradation also does not remove the full performance cost: the plan-conditioning interface retains a baseline grasp-rate penalty of 0.2740.274. Third, we validated the redundancy principle across three causal manipulations: an ambiguity sweep, an occlusion sweep, and the LIBERO counterfactual test. We do not yet know whether the same principle extends to other robot task families or to reasoning VLAs more broadly.

8 Conclusion

We investigate where multimodality should live in a reasoning-augmented VLA. A generative action model can represent multiple motor trajectories without preserving distinct task-level choices. GPL instead represents the intermediate decision as a distribution over plans, keeping those alternatives available before execution. This makes the reasoning state addressable: valid decisions can be sampled, a requested one can be selected, and deployment outcomes can change which alternatives are preferred without retraining the underlying VLA.

Across our experiments, the plan distribution provides a stronger control interface than language prompting or intervention on π0\pi_{0}’s native action distribution. The same representation also supports adaptation from experience. Finally, the redundancy principle clarifies when this interface should matter: an explicit plan becomes consequential when it carries decision information that the observation does not already determine. Together, these results suggest that intermediate reasoning in VLAs should be designed not only to encode a decision; it must establish addressability, exposing the full space of viable alternatives over which that decision can still be made.

Appendix A Theory and Related-Work Comparison

A.1 A Committed Regression Readout Mode-Averages

Proposition 1 (A committed regression readout mode-averages)

Let cc denote the conditioning information and let z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} denote a plan drawn from p⁡(z∣c)p(z\mid c). A deterministic readout z^​(c)\hat{z}(c) trained with squared error, minz^⁡𝔼c,z​‖z^​(c)−z‖22\min_{\hat{z}}\mathbb{E}_{c,z}\|\hat{z}(c)-z\|_{2}^{2}, has population minimizer z^∗​(c)=𝔼⁡[z∣c]≡zdet\hat{z}^{*}(c)=\mathbb{E}[z\mid c]\equiv z_{\text{det}}. Suppose that, for a fixed cc, the valid plans are the distinct modes {z1,…,zm}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\}, with m≥2m\geq 2 and probabilities πi>0\pi_{i}>0. Then

zdet=∑i=1mπi​zi∈conv⁡{z1,…,zm},z_{\text{det}}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\pi_{i}z_{i}\in\operatorname{conv}\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\}, (4)

and if the modes are affinely independent (in particular, whenever m=2m=2), this strict convex combination is not itself a valid mode: zdet∉{z1,…,zm}z_{\text{det}}\notin\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\} and Δ⁡(c)≡mini⁡‖zdet−zi‖2>0\Delta(c)\equiv\min_{i}\left\|z_{\text{det}}-z_{i}\right\|_{2}>0.

Corollary 1 (What a committed point cannot expose)

For a fixed observation, a deterministic plan readout exposes at most one of mm valid modes, with zero probability mass on any other; by Proposition 1, that one point can itself be the invalid mean. There is therefore nothing for plan-level reweighting (steering) or outcome adaptation (reranking) to act on.

Appendix B Setup and Reproducibility

Gives the full reproducibility record referenced throughout the main text: the GPL training and sampling recipe (Section B.1), how a pretrained VLA is adapted to receive a plan (Section B.2), the matched LaRA-style baseline (Section B.3), and the learned-coordinate control (Section B.4).

B.1 GPL Training and Sampling

GPL models a distribution over task-level plans rather than directly over actions. Training is performed entirely offline from pairs (c,z)(c,z), where cc is a frozen representation of the current observation and instruction and zz is a low-dimensional plan extracted from the corresponding demonstration.

Conditioning representation.

For each observation–instruction pair, we run the frozen reasoning backbone once with hidden-state outputs enabled and cache the last transformer’s final-token representation,

c=fϕ​(o,l)∈ℝdmodel.c=f_{\phi}(o,l)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}}.

These features are precomputed for the complete training set and stored offline. GPL training therefore does not require backpropagation through the pretrained VLA.

Rectified-flow generator.

Let z∈ℝdzz\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} denote the plan extracted from a demonstration. We train a conditional velocity field vθ​(zt,t,c)v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c) using rectified flow. For

z0∼𝒩⁡(0,I),t∼𝒰⁡[0,1],zt=(1−t)​z0+t​z,z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),\qquad t\sim\mathcal{U}[0,1],\qquad z_{t}=(1-t)z_{0}+tz,

the training objective is

ℒGPL=𝔼[‖vθ(zt,t,c)−(z−z0)‖]22.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GPL}}=\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|{}v_{\theta}(z_{t},t,c)-(z-z_{0})\right\|{}_{2}^{2}\right].

The conditioning vector is first projected from dmodeld_{\text{model}} to 64 dimensions using a linear layer, LayerNorm, and GELU. Time is represented with a 64-dimensional sinusoidal embedding. The noisy plan, time embedding, and projected conditioning vector are concatenated and passed through a two-hidden-layer MLP with width 256 and SiLU activations:

[dz+64+64]→256→256→dz.[d_{z}+64+64]\rightarrow 256\rightarrow 256\rightarrow d_{z}.

Table 3 summarizes the full recipe.

Sampling.

At inference time, we initialize z0∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and numerically integrate the learned velocity field from t=0t=0 to t=1t=1 using Euler updates,

zi+1=zi+Δ​t​vθ​(zi,ti,c).z_{i+1}=z_{i}+\Delta t\,v_{\theta}(z_{i},t_{i},c).

Unless otherwise noted, we use a fixed-step Euler solver with n=4n=4 steps for GPL sampling. When applying classifier guidance, we increase the number of integration steps to n∈{6,8}n\in\{6,8\} to allow the guidance gradient sufficient iterations to effectively steer the generation.

B.2 VLA Adaptation and Plan Injection

We condition the pretrained VLA on a plan latent zz through learned soft tokens while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen. The dimensionality of zz is task-dependent; examples used in our experiments include object position, grasp orientation, and higher-dimensional contact sketches. The conditioning mechanism itself is independent of this dimensionality.

Plan projection and injection.

A small MLP PηP_{\eta} maps the plan latent to k=8k=8 embeddings with the same width as the VLA prefix:

Pη:ℝdz→ℝ8×2048.P_{\eta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{8\times 2048}.

Concretely, the projector consists of

dz→512→512→×2048,d_{z}\rightarrow 512\rightarrow 512\rightarrow 8\!\times\!2048,

with SiLU nonlinearities between linear layers. The resulting embeddings are appended to the image–language prefix constructed by the pretrained PaliGemma backbone (Beyer et al., 2024). They participate in the same bidirectional prefix attention as the original image and language tokens. The same modified prefix construction is used during both training and action sampling, so no separate inference-time conditioning mechanism is required.

All parameters of the pretrained VLA are frozen. We optimize the plan projector together with a lightweight LoRA adaptation of the action expert. Training uses the VLA’s original flow-matching objective, with no additional plan-specific loss. The precise checkpoint, LoRA parameterization, and optimization hyperparameters are domain-specific and are reported in Table 4. With probability pdropp_{\mathrm{drop}}, the plan is omitted during training, providing a classifier-free anchor to the plan-less policy (Classifier-free guidance, Ho & Salimans (2022)).

B.2.1 Variations of the π0\pi_{0} Baseline

When evaluating GPL against π0\pi_{0}, we compare it against one of three distinct baseline configurations:

  • •

    Stock π0\pi_{0}: The unmodified base model.

  • •

    Matched plan-less control: The GPL model evaluated with the plan tokens omitted.

  • •

    Dedicated no-plan adapter: The stock π0\pi_{0} model fine-tuned for the target task via LoRA, without plan generation.

Crucially, these configurations are not interchangeable. As demonstrated on the two-cube grasp task (Table 5), simply dropping the plan from GPL (the matched plan-less control) severely degrades performance and does not recover the behavior of the stock model. To ensure a rigorous evaluation, our experiments consistently compare GPL against the strongest of these baselines for each specific test.

B.3 LaRA-Style Matched Baseline

We implement a LaRA-style matched baseline with a deterministic continuous reasoning latent followed by a generative flow action head, matched to our own conditioning, action-head shape, and evaluation task rather than reproducing LaRA-VLA’s original benchmark end to end. Given conditioning features cc, the reasoning module produces a single latent hrh_{r} through a two-layer MLP and additionally predicts a visual latent using the auxiliary visual-CoT objective. The action module is a rectified-flow network conditioned on the resulting deterministic reasoning representation h^\hat{h}, and is sampled with four Euler steps. We preserve LaRA-VLA’s core architectural claim, a deterministic, Coconut-style continuous thought token conditioning a generative action head, trained with its reported three-stage curriculum and visual-CoT auxiliary objective, and adapt the reasoning dimensionality, task domain, and training budget to this paper’s own bimodal manipulation substrate and evaluation metrics.

Training follows a three-stage curriculum:

ℒ1\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{1} =ℒplan+0.1​ℒvis,\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{plan}}+0.1\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}},
ℒ2\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{2} =0.3​ℒplan+0.2​ℒvis+ℒflow,\displaystyle=0.3\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{plan}}+0.2\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}},
ℒ3\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{3} =ℒflow+0.05​ℒvis,\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}}+0.05\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}},

where ℒplan\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{plan}} is MSE on the deterministic reasoning target, ℒvis\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vis}} is an L1L_{1} visual-latent prediction loss against an exponential-moving-average (EMA) target encoder (τ=0.99\tau=0.99), and ℒflow\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{flow}} is the same rectified-flow velocity-matching objective used for GPL. Table 6 lists the full recipe.

For mode-coverage evaluation, we sample K=16K=16 actions for each held-out condition and count a mode as recovered when a committed sample falls within 0.030.03 of the corresponding target. For reasoning-level steering, we apply the same guidance classifier and protocol used for GPL directly to LaRA’s deterministic reasoning latent, isolating the effect of replacing a sampled plan distribution with a single continuous thought representation.

B.4 Learned Plan Coordinates

To test whether addressability depends on hand-designed plan coordinates, we learn a plan representation directly from demonstrated end-effector motion. For each demonstration, we sample the End-Effector Position (EEP) at 16 uniformly spaced future phases, express each position relative to the current EEP, and flatten the resulting trajectory to x∈ℝ48x\in\mathbb{R}^{48}. No object identity, mode label, or language supervision is used to construct this representation.

We fit a deterministic autoencoder

48→128→2→128→4848\rightarrow 128\rightarrow 2\rightarrow 128\rightarrow 48

with SiLU activations and reconstruction MSE. Raw trajectories are normalized using the mean and population standard deviation of the corresponding outer-training fold; the resulting 2-D latent codes are standardized again using statistics computed only from the same training fold. The encoder is then frozen, and these standardized codes replace the hand-designed plan coordinates in the same generative-flow and deterministic-plan models used in the main experiments. Table 7 lists the full training configuration.

Appendix C Evaluating Generality: The Maze Navigation Domain

While the primary focus of this work is robotic manipulation, we also evaluate GPL on a 2D maze navigation task to demonstrate its generality.

We build upon the easy-to-hard maze framework of Schwarzschild et al. (2021). The architecture processes a 3-channel maze image alongside the agent’s current cell coordinate. Following our standard recipe, the model first diffuses a plan (represented as a 144-dimensional downsampled solution-path image for size-9 mazes) and then autoregresses a sequence of discrete moves conditioned on this generated latent plan.

Because the original dataset features only single-solution mazes, we developed a custom data generator to create environments with multiple equal-cost, interior-disjoint routes (e.g., a ring, a staircase of two non-crossing paths, and a comb of K>2K>2 corridors). This ensures that the target plan distribution is genuinely multimodal at decision forks, and that training and testing sets are strictly disjoint. We train three model variants on identical data: our generative plan model, a standard no-plan baseline, and a deterministic twin that regresses the plan using squared error combined with action cross-entropy.

We evaluate these models on held-out mazes across three key capabilities, demonstrating the distinct advantages of the generative approach (Figure 7).

C.1 Maze-Domain Implementation Details

The maze experiments use a separate architecture from the manipulation experiments. All variants share a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style maze encoder and an autoregressive GPT-2 move decoder over the four discrete actions {up, down, left, right}. The encoder has width 256, depth 6, head dimension 64, RoPE positional encoding, and no dropout. The generative and deterministic plan models additionally predict the same 144-D plan representation obtained by bilinearly downsampling the solution-path image by a factor of two, flattening it, and applying L2L_{2} normalization. The no-plan baseline bypasses this representation and predicts moves directly from the shared backbone. Table 8 gives the full recipe.

Generative plan model.

The maze gpl instantiation uses continuous-time diffusion rather than rectified flow. We use a cosine log-SNR schedule with γmin=−15\gamma_{\min}=-15 and γmax=15\gamma_{\max}=15. Training times t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] are importance-sampled using an EMA loss-weighted sampler over 100 log-SNR bins. At inference, plans are generated with DDIM-style (Song et al., 2020) sampling using 50 denoising steps; this value is fixed explicitly by all evaluation scripts.

Dataset and action horizon.

We generate 4000 size-9 mazes for each topology with strictly disjoint training and test sets. Ring mazes contain two equal-length routes around a rectangular ring, while staircase mazes contain two interior-disjoint winding routes. The default autoregressive horizon is T=8T=8 moves. Staircase experiments use T=16T=16, since the longer routes cannot be executed reliably within eight moves; this keeps closed-loop task completion from confounding the plan-coverage comparison.

Steering and outcome adaptation.

Steering uses a noise-conditioned route classifier p⁡(y∣zt,α2)p(y\mid z_{t},\alpha^{2}), trained for 3000 steps, whose log-probability gradient is added during diffusion sampling. Guidance strength is swept over s∈{0,4,8,16,32}s\in\{0,4,8,16,32\}. Outcome adaptation keeps the diffusion generator frozen and fits a binary success critic to accumulated (z,r)(z,r) pairs collected from execution. Candidate plans are then reranked with Boltzmann weights proportional to exp⁡(β​g​(z))\exp(\beta\,g(z)).

Evaluation protocol.

Coverage draws K=16K=16 plans at each fork and evaluates closed-loop replanning on 200 held-out mazes. Steering is evaluated on 100 held-out mazes over the guidance sweep above. Outcome adaptation uses the hidden route-reliability intervention and 100 held-out test mazes. Reported confidence intervals capture variation across held-out mazes; each model variant is trained from a single training seed per maze family.

Appendix D Separating Mode Averaging from Addressability

The deterministic MSE baseline confounds two effects: it can regress toward an invalid conditional mean, and at inference time it exposes only a single plan. We therefore construct a stronger deterministic model that explicitly learns multiple valid modes and use it to isolate the second effect. Crucially, we compare two inference read-outs of the same trained model: one exposes only a single mode, while the other preserves access to the learned alternatives.

Multi-hypothesis deterministic model.

Given conditioning cc, the model predicts M=4M=4 candidate plan means {μm​(c)}m=1M\{\mu_{m}(c)\}_{m=1}^{M} together with categorical logits over the candidates. It is trained with WTA multiple-choice regression (Guzmán-Rivera et al., 2012; Rupprecht et al., 2017):

ℒ=1B​∑bminm⁡‖μm​(cb)−zb‖22+CE⁡(logits⁡(cb),arg⁡minm⁡‖μm​(cb)−zb‖22).\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b}\min_{m}\left\|\mu_{m}(c_{b})-z_{b}\right\|_{2}^{2}+\mathrm{CE}\!\left(\mathrm{logits}(c_{b}),\arg\min_{m}\left\|\mu_{m}(c_{b})-z_{b}\right\|_{2}^{2}\right). (5)

The first term lets different candidates specialize to different valid plans, while the second learns their categorical probabilities. We use M=4M=4, deliberately larger than the two ground-truth modes, so the model is not given the correct mode count. Conditioning encoder, trunk, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, and training budget match the deterministic twin.

Same weights, different read-outs.

After training, we evaluate two inference interfaces without updating any weights:

  • •

    WTA, MAP: return only the mean of the highest-probability component. The model may have learned several valid modes internally, but only one is accessible at inference time.

  • •

    WTA, component sampled: sample a component index from the predicted categorical distribution and return its mean. The same learned modes are now individually accessible across repeated draws.

This comparison therefore changes only whether the alternatives already encoded in the model remain addressable at inference time.

For steering, the sampled read-out can be commanded by selecting the desired component, whereas the MAP read-out has no corresponding degree of freedom. For reranking, we report rerank feasibility: the fraction of layouts for which the K=16K=16 candidate set contains at least one zero-cost plan under an oracle reranker. This measures whether a useful alternative is present in the candidate set, independently of critic accuracy.

The result separates mode averaging from addressability (Table 9). The WTA model already avoids the invalid conditional mean by learning multiple candidate plans. Nevertheless, MAP inference still collapses those learned alternatives to a single exposed plan, giving zero coverage and zero steering range. Changing only the read-out to component sampling recovers coverage, steerability, and full reranking feasibility. Thus, avoiding mode averaging is not sufficient: the learned alternatives must also remain accessible at inference time.

We therefore treat the WTA experiment as a positive control for the addressability hypothesis rather than as a competing method. It shows that the same property can arise from a discrete mixture representation: rectified flow is not uniquely required. gpl instead provides a continuous plan distribution without requiring a predefined component count MM, while supporting the same sampling, steering, and outcome-reweighting interface.

Appendix E Steering: Where the Handle Acts

Supports the steering results of Section 4.2: where guidance is most effective under a shared executor (Section E.1), the protocol behind the native-π0\pi_{0} action-chunk comparison (Section E.2), and the full language-steering baseline comparison (Section E.3).

E.1 Full Steering-Locus Comparison

First, we isolate the locus of intervention using a shared soft-token executor (a flow-matching action model trained from scratch). To ensure a fair comparison, the plan and action branches share the exact same task, layouts, and guidance objective; the only variable is the representation being guided. We additionally compare against a LaRA-style baseline. Although its downstream action head is generative, its deterministic reasoning token yields a steer range of nearly zero. As Figure 8 demonstrates, the plan representation serves as a substantially stronger locus for steering.

E.2 Guidance on the Native High-Dimensional Action Chunk

This section gives the protocol behind the main-text comparison in Figure 3: how guidance doses are made comparable across representations and how discriminator capacity is matched between the plan and action-chunk arms.

The main-text comparison with π0\pi_{0} evaluates each intervention through its native executor. The plan arm uses the plan-conditioned adapter, whereas the action arm uses a dedicated no-plan adapter trained at the same adaptation budget. Each arm receives its own discriminator: plan guidance differentiates with respect to the noisy plan ztz_{t}, while action guidance trains the requested-mode classifier on that adapter’s noisy native action chunk and differentiates with respect to xt∈ℝ4×32x_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times 32}.

This is therefore a matched-system comparison rather than a causal isolation of locus alone. As a diagnostic, the commanded cube is explicit in the 3-D plan, whereas held-out balanced accuracy for decoding it from the action chunk is 0.570.57, 0.570.57, and 0.490.49 across the three train/evaluation pairings. Thus the comparison measures the effectiveness of the two native intervention interfaces; it does not establish that representation dimensionality alone causes the difference.

Making the guidance doses comparable.

A raw classifier-gradient magnitude is not directly comparable across representations with different dimensionality and scale. We therefore normalize each guidance displacement by the corresponding Euler-step length:

xt+Δ​t=xt+Δ​t​vt+w⁡‖Δ​t​vt‖​∇xt​log​qψ​(y∣xt,t)‖∇xt​log​qψ​(y∣xt,t)‖.x_{t+\Delta t}=x_{t}+\Delta t\,v_{t}+w\,\left\|\Delta t\,v_{t}\right\|\,\frac{\nabla_{x_{t}}\log q_{\psi}(y\mid x_{t},t)}{\left\|\nabla_{x_{t}}\log q_{\psi}(y\mid x_{t},t)\right\|}. (6)

With this parameterization, ww is dimensionless and w=0w=0 recovers the unguided sampler in both arms.

E.3 Language Steering Under a Shared Executor

We next compare the latent plan against natural language as an alternative command channel. To ensure any differences are due to the command channel and not downstream execution capability, we train a single shared executor per seed on the two-cube task. This executor exposes three independently maskable command channels. During evaluation, each arm activates only its own channel and nulls the others, and all arms are scored using the same closed-loop outcome.

We compare the plan against three language baselines:

  • •

    L-stock: A frozen ECoT model decodes a cube choice and routes that decision to the shared downstream executor.

  • •

    L-prefix: The named instruction is provided directly as text in the shared executor’s own LM prefix, with no separate reasoner or learned projector.

  • •

    L-soft: Projects a 40964096-D sentence feature into the exact same eight-soft-token interface used by the plan. This has 12.27% more trainable parameters than the gpl projector, ensuring the plan does not win simply due to parameter capacity.

Execution versus steering. L-stock provides the most interpretable language baseline because execution competence does not limit it. It achieves the highest overall grasp rate (0.500.50), yet its steer-range interval contains zero on two of the three seeds (Table 10). This indicates that while L-stock is physically capable of the task, it largely ignores the language command. In contrast, the plan (gpl) successfully steers execution.

L-soft failure. While L-soft provides a fair architectural control, its grasp rate collapsed to 0.060.06 at this data scale. Because it rarely grasps anything, its steer range cannot serve as a reliable measure of information transfer.

Guidance dose. For the language channels evaluated here, preliminary dose calibration showed only a narrow useful extrapolation range (peaking near w=0.5w=0.5 and collapsing by w=1.0w=1.0). Therefore, we report the plain conditional performance for each language channel rather than selecting a guidance dose on the evaluation set.

Appendix F Outcome Adaptation and the Compute Frontier

Supports the outcome-adaptation results of Section 4.3: the reranking protocol, its cost validation, where reranking should act, and the compute-frontier measurement. The frontier is measured on the controlled two-cube task rather than through π0\pi_{0}, and we do not extrapolate its ratio to the π0\pi_{0} experiments.

F.1 Additional Outcome Adaptation Details

This section formalizes the outcome-adaptation mechanism sketched in Section 3: the reweighted-distribution estimator and the scoring functions used across the outcome-adaptation experiments.

The main text treats outcome adaptation as the general operation of reweighting samples from a frozen plan distribution using deployment feedback. Over the finite candidate set, the reweighted distribution of Equation 3 is implemented as

ρk=exp⁡(β​s​(c,z(k)))∑j=1Kexp⁡(β​s​(c,z(j))),z⋆∼Categorical⁡(ρ1,…,ρK).\rho_{k}=\frac{\exp\!\left(\beta s(c,z^{(k)})\right)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp\!\left(\beta s(c,z^{(j)})\right)},\qquad z^{\star}\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{K}). (7)

Reporting convention. Instead of executing a single sampled plan z⋆z^{\star}, all results in this paper report the Boltzmann-weighted expected outcome evaluated exactly over the sampled pool:

V^​(c)=𝔼z⋆∼Categorical⁡(ρ)​[r⋆]=∑k=1Kρk​r(k).\hat{V}(c)=\mathbb{E}_{z^{\star}\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\rho)}[r^{\star}]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\rho_{k}\,r^{(k)}. (8)

Here, r(k)r^{(k)} is the observed outcome (e.g., a success bit, path cost, or preference indicator) associated with candidate z(k)z^{(k)}. This approach applies uniformly to all three scoring methods below. It provides a lower-variance estimate than a single physical draw, though it requires knowing the actual outcome for all KK candidates rather than just the one deployed.

Learned critic.

We fit a scalar regressor gω:ℝdz→ℝg_{\omega}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R} to the accumulated (z(k),r(k))(z^{(k)},r^{(k)}) pairs observed at deployment, using a supervised loss matched to the outcome type (binary cross-entropy for a success bit, squared error for a scalar cost), and set s⁡(c,z)=gω​(z)s(c,z)=g_{\omega}(z). Because gωg_{\omega} is continuous in zz, it can score plans that were never directly observed, at the cost of the fitting compute.

Reward table.

When the outcome space admits a natural finite partition of the plan into MM discrete modes through a mode map m:ℝdz→{1,…,M}m:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\{1,\ldots,M\} (e.g., which object, route, or order a candidate plan resolves to), the score can instead be read directly off observed outcomes in that mode:

s⁡(c,z)=r¯m⁡(z),r¯j=∑i=1N𝟙[m(z(i))=j]r(i)+κnj+2​κ,s(c,z)=\bar{r}_{m(z)},\qquad\bar{r}_{j}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}[m(z^{(i)})=j]\,r^{(i)}+\kappa}{n_{j}+2\kappa}, (9)

where njn_{j} is the number of observed rollouts assigned to mode jj and κ>0\kappa>0 is a Jeffreys/Laplace pseudo-count keeping r¯j\bar{r}_{j} finite before mode jj has been observed (κ=0.5\kappa=0.5 throughout). This score costs zero training FLOPs, since it is a running average rather than a fitted function, but it can only distinguish plans across the modes the partition resolves.

F.2 Where Should Outcome-Based Reranking Act?

To rigorously isolate the locus of reranking, we compare the plan arm against a dedicated no-plan adapter (Section B.2.1), matching the architecture, optimizer, rank, and step budget to avoid the degradation of a network simply run without its plan. Both LoRA adapters are hot-swapped in a single process, sharing identical scenes, backbones, execution trajectories, and per-candidate action-noise seeds.

As discussed in the main text, the performance gap between plan- and action-level reranking stems from executable diversity (Figure 9, left). While the action arm achieves comparable raw candidate coverage at higher budgets, its draws successfully grasp at less than half the rate of the plan arm. Because the action sampler rarely produces independent, successful alternatives, the downstream reranking outcomes differ significantly depending on the objective (Figure 9, right). For the PATH objective (total end-effector Euclidean distance), plan-level reranking significantly reduces execution cost while action-level reranking does not, and this advantage widens with the sample budget KK. Conversely, both arms perform similarly on the FIELD objective (a smooth Gaussian cost bump centered on one of the two cube locations in the scene), where cost relies on localized spatial avoidance rather than being tightly coupled to the initial mode choice.

F.3 Compute-Frontier Protocol

This section specifies the success–training-FLOPs comparison in Section 4.3: two frozen-gpl outcome-adaptation variants, continued behavior cloning, and AWR (Peng et al., 2019).

Task and evaluation.

We use the two-cube reliability task, in which one grasp mode succeeds with probability 0.90.9 and the other with probability 0.250.25. These reliabilities are hidden from the policy; after each executed grasp, the environment returns only a binary success/failure outcome. All arms start from the same conditioning cache, plan-latent flow, deterministic twin, and flow-action executor, and differ only in how deployment outcomes are used.

At every round, performance is measured as the Boltzmann-weighted expected success rate over the sampled plan pool (Equation 8). We evaluate two forms of outcome adaptation. gpl + critic learns a score model from accumulated deployment outcomes, while gpl + reward table directly estimates the empirical success probability of each discrete mode. The latter is applicable here because the two plan modes correspond directly to the left and right cube. It reaches a final SR statistically indistinguishable from the learned critic while requiring no score-model training (Figure 4B).

Compared arms.

The four strategies are summarized in Table 11. Continued BC and AWR update their flow cumulatively across five deployment rounds, with no reset between rounds. For every arm, we additionally evaluate a shuffled-outcome control in which observed rewards are randomly reassigned to sampled plans. These controls test whether improvement depends on the correspondence between a plan and its observed outcome rather than arising from reranking or continued optimization alone.

FLOP accounting.

Training cost is estimated with the standard proxy:

FLOPs=6​Nparams​Nsamples​processed,\mathrm{FLOPs}=6\,N_{\mathrm{params}}\,N_{\mathrm{samples\ processed}},

and accumulated over all optimizer steps and deployment rounds. gpl + reward table incurs exactly zero training FLOPs, while gpl + critic pays only for fitting the ∼17\sim 17k-parameter critic. Continued BC and AWR repeatedly update the larger flow and therefore each consume 388×388\times the training FLOPs of the critic-based gpl arm, yielding the ratio reported in Figure 4B.

Because the models in this controlled experiment are deliberately small, we interpret this comparison as a relative compute frontier under a common FLOP proxy rather than an absolute systems benchmark. We do not report wall-clock time, and the 388×388\times ratio is specific to this task; we do not extrapolate it to the π0\pi_{0} experiments.

Appendix G The Redundancy Score and the LIBERO Counterfactual Test

This section develops and validates the redundancy score R~\widetilde{R} presented in Section 5.

G.1 Counterfactual Intervention

We first test whether reducing redundancy makes the plan more influential. The original scene demonstrations partially couple the visual scene to the demonstrated decision. We replace them with counterfactual pairs in which opposing decisions occur in the same visual context. This removes the observation-decision correlation from the plan-training data. The executor, benchmark, adaptation procedure, and six adapter seeds remain unchanged.

Adding counterfactual scenes makes the plan substantially more relevant to the decision without degrading the overall competence of the policy (Table 12).

G.2 Estimating Redundancy

To ensure our conclusions are not dependent on a specific metric, we estimate the redundancy score using three different methods:

  • •

    E1: The preregistered L2 logistic probe with fixed regularization (used for the main text endpoints).

  • •

    E2: The same probe with regularization selected by inner grouped cross-validation and calibrated probabilities.

  • •

    E3: A non-parametric grouped five-fold kk-NN conditional-entropy estimate (k=25k=25, cosine distance).

We replace a fraction qq of the original scenes (drawn once per scene with common random numbers, so the five levels are nested) with their counterfactual counterparts, creating five matched demonstration mixtures, where q=0q=0 denotes the original scenes and q=1q=1 the fully counterfactual set. While the absolute magnitudes vary, all three estimators preserve the exact same redundancy ordering across demonstration sets (Table 13).

The results in Table 13 demonstrate a continuous relationship: decreasing redundancy correlates perfectly with increased steering (Spearman’s ρ=−1.00\rho=-1.00). Methodologically, this dose-response sweep isolates six tasks and samples exactly one record per usable training episode. In contrast, the baseline in Table 12 spans ten tasks and retains every logged conditioning vector, including repeated physical attempts at the same scene.

Appendix H Generality Across Plan Representations and Domains

H.1 A Shared 54-D Contact Sketch

We evaluate a shared plan representation across four SimplerEnv task families with qualitatively different decision ambiguities:

  • •

    pick-and-place, where a generic instruction leaves two identical cubes as valid targets;

  • •

    grasp-yaw, where a square-footprint cube admits two valid grasp orientations;

  • •

    can pick-or-push, where the same target can be reached through carrying or pushing;

  • •

    sweep, a symmetric non-prehensile task in which debris can be pushed toward either of two identical corners.

To represent these decisions through one interface, we use a shared 54-D contact sketch with six object slots and nine channels per slot: object-relative contact position, approach direction, and contact state. Unused slots are padded and overflow objects are truncated by a fixed rule. Different families therefore express their decision through different components of the same representation: pick-and-place and grasp-yaw primarily through contact position and approach direction, can pick-or-push through gripper and surface-contact state, and sweep through target contact geometry.

Despite this shared representation, a single jointly trained reasoner preserves addressability across all four families (Figure 10).

A strategy-level deployment shift.

Can pick-or-push provides a particularly direct example because the two modes correspond to different physical strategies. The reasoner is trained only on small cans (diameters 29.729.7–36.336.3 mm), for which both carrying and pushing are viable, while deployment changes only the can diameter. Although the WidowX gripper opens wider than these objects, grasping becomes limited by the approach geometry: as the can widens, the open fingers collide with it during the descending pick approach and topple it before the close command.

We verify this mechanism directly. At a 39.639.6 mm diameter, the can remains upright after the lateral reach in all 2020 instrumented episodes, but crosses the tipping threshold during the subsequent descent in all 2020, before any gripper-close command. Pushing avoids this approach and remains viable. The frozen generator nevertheless continues to propose both strategies on shifted scenes. The deployment outcomes therefore change which existing plan is preferred, rather than requiring a new strategy to be learned (Figure 10).

Scene-dependent shifts across task families.

We apply a physical intervention that selectively disables one alternative in each family. Pick-and-place enlarges one cube beyond the usable grasp geometry; grasp-yaw introduces a barrier along one grasp axis; can pick-or-push uses the size intervention analyzed above; and sweep places a lip across the approach to one target corner.

For pick-and-place, grasp-yaw, and sweep, the disabled alternative is randomized independently across scenes. Consequently, neither mode has a globally higher marginal reward: successful adaptation requires predicting which alternative remains viable in the current scene. The can shift instead induces a persistent preference for pushing across deployment scenes. Together, these settings distinguish scene-conditioned adaptation from learning a single global mode preference. Table 14 reports the per-family scene and rollout counts.

Protocol details.

The shared evaluation protocol is summarized in Table 15.

H.2 Cross-Simulator Battery

RoboCasa changes the simulator and scene distribution, while retaining the same plan interface and pretrained π0\pi_{0} executor. Figure 11 reports coverage, steering, and outcome adaptation under this shift. Coverage there tests that π0\pi_{0} realizes both commanded directions; the deterministic twin is the midpoint anchor, and the adaptation prior draws anchors uniformly between the two sides.
